description: TEEs and enclaves (Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone, TDX, SEV), attestation, and confidential computing.

ndss.narrative:
Trusted execution environment research at NDSS has tracked the rapid evolution of TEE architectures from the SGX and TrustZone era through ARM CCA and AMD SEV. ZeroTrace (NDSS 2018) established early that SGX alone does not prevent access-pattern leakage and proposed oblivious RAM as a necessary complement. SANCTUARY (NDSS 2019) then pushed TrustZone enclaves down to user-space applications on mobile SoCs, dramatically widening the attack surface that TEE defenses must cover.

Custos (NDSS 2020) used SGX to provide tamper-evident auditing of the operating system itself, inverting the typical trust assumption that the OS protects the enclave. CHANCEL (NDSS 2021) addressed the multi-client setting, providing efficient isolation even when adversarial programs share an enclave's execution context.

The 2022–2025 papers reflect both the mainstreaming of TEEs and the discovery of new attack vectors against them. Hybrid Trust MPC (NDSS 2022) used TEEs as trust anchors within larger multi-party computation protocols; CAGE (NDSS 2024) proposed GPU extensions to ARM CCA for confidential ML workloads; and CounterSEVeillance (NDSS 2025) showed that performance-counter leakage in AMD SEV-SNP remains an open problem even in the most modern confidential computing designs. The community's focus has broadened from CPU microarchitecture to the entire silicon ecosystem.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list reflect a field reckoning with the fragility of hardware enclaves just as they reached mainstream processors. Foreshadow (USENIX 2018) was a watershed, showing that transient out-of-order execution could extract the very attestation keys underpinning Intel SGX, while The Guard's Dilemma (USENIX 2018) demonstrated practical code-reuse attacks against enclave code itself. Parallel work questioned other roots of trust, with A Bad Dream (USENIX 2018) subverting the Trusted Platform Module via power-management states. The early message was clear: the hardware promised isolation, but its microarchitectural and lifecycle assumptions leaked.

A second wave broadened the attack and defense surface beyond SGX. Researchers turned to ARM TrustZone, with PARTEMU (USENIX 2020) enabling dynamic analysis of real-world trusted OSes and Horizontal Privilege Escalation in Trusted Applications (USENIX 2020) exposing weak isolation between trusted apps. At the same time, tooling matured for finding enclave bugs systematically, from TeeRex (USENIX 2020) discovering memory-corruption in SGX enclaves to SGXFuzz (USENIX 2022) synthesizing nested input structures for fuzzing. A complementary thread treated the host-enclave boundary as adversarial in both directions, as in SGXLock and SGXLock's mutual-distrust model and A Hardware-Software Co-design for Efficient Intra-Enclave Isolation (both USENIX 2022). Builders also began delivering real confidential-computing systems, such as Visor (USENIX 2020) for private video analytics and Civet (USENIX 2020) for partitioning Java into enclaves.

The center of gravity then shifted toward confidential VMs and AMD SEV. CIPHERLEAKS (USENIX 2021) introduced the ciphertext side channel that broke constant-time crypto on SEV, and VoltPillager (USENIX 2021) revived hardware fault injection against SGX via voltage scaling. This line continued into recent attacks on VM-granularity TEEs, with HECKLER (USENIX 2024) weaponizing malicious interrupts and CacheWarp (USENIX 2024) using selective state reset as software fault injection. Defensively, the field moved from patching to principled assurance, including formally verified hypervisor memory protection (USENIX 2021), DICE* (USENIX 2021) for verified measured boot, and AEX-Notify (USENIX 2023), a co-designed mitigation for precise single-stepping adopted into Intel SGX.

Today the area spans new hardware abstractions and richer use cases. SHELTER (USENIX 2023) extends Arm CCA with user-space isolation, ReZone (USENIX 2022) reduces TrustZone TEE privilege, and attestation work scales to fleets and real-time systems, as in SCRAPS (USENIX 2022) for pub-sub IoT and ARI (USENIX 2023) for mission-execution integrity. Confidential computing has also become a deployment substrate, with Reusable Enclaves (USENIX 2023) targeting serverless workloads. The arc runs from demonstrating that enclaves leak, to building tools and systems around them, to defending VM-scale TEEs with formal methods and hardware-software co-design.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, clustered around 2018, established the two faces of Trusted Execution Environments: building useful systems on top of enclaves, and tearing those enclaves apart. On the constructive side, S&P 2018's "EnclaveDB: A Secure Database Using SGX" and NDSS 2018's "ZeroTrace: Oblivious Memory Primitives from Intel SGX" and "OBLIVIATE: A Data Oblivious Filesystem for Intel SGX" showed that SGX could host real applications (databases, oblivious storage) while defending against the access-pattern leakage that plagues enclave memory. On the destructive side, "Foreshadow" (USENIX 2018) was the watershed: a transient out-of-order execution attack that extracted SGX's attestation keys, undermining the entire trust chain. CCS 2018's "Nemesis" and S&P 2018's "Racing in Hyperspace" rounded out the early threat picture by mining interrupt-timing and hyper-threading side channels, the latter offering a defensive tool (HyperRace) rather than just an attack.

By 2019 the field broadened along two axes: new architectures and new attack classes. NDSS 2019 pushed enclaves beyond Intel with "SANCTUARY: ARMing TrustZone with User-space Enclaves" and "TIMBER-V" (bringing fine-grained enclaves to RISC-V), while CCS 2019's "SecTEE" explored software-based enclave architectures. At the same time, attackers turned to the analog and software-runtime layers: "VoltJockey" (CCS 2019) breached TrustZone by manipulating CPU voltage, "Hardware-Backed Heist" (CCS 2019) extracted ECDSA keys from Qualcomm's TrustZone, and "A Tale of Two Worlds" (CCS 2019) systematized the vulnerabilities lurking in the enclave/host interface itself. Defensive responses appeared in parallel — "Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX" (CCS 2019) — alongside applications like "LightBox" and "Tesseract."

The 2020-2021 era was dominated by physical and microarchitectural fault and side-channel attacks that broke the assumption hardware could be trusted from software. "Plundervolt" (S&P 2020) and later "VoltPillager" (USENIX 2021) injected faults via voltage scaling; "LVI" (S&P 2020) inverted Spectre to inject malicious data into enclaves; "PLATYPUS" (S&P 2021) leaked secrets through software-readable power measurements. The center of gravity also shifted toward VM-level confidential computing on AMD SEV, which proved repeatedly fragile: "SEVurity" (S&P 2020), "CIPHERLEAKS" (USENIX 2021), "CrossLine" (CCS 2021), and "One Glitch to Rule Them All" (CCS 2021) each broke SEV's memory-encryption or isolation guarantees. "SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems" (S&P 2020) and "TeeRex" (USENIX 2020) consolidated this knowledge into systematic and tooling form, and "On the TOCTOU Problem in Remote Attestation" (CCS 2021) sharpened attestation's foundations.

By 2022 the area had matured into a confidential-computing discipline grappling with structural, hard-to-patch leaks and entirely new TEE form factors. "A Systematic Look at Ciphertext Side Channels on AMD SEV-SNP" (S&P 2022) showed that even SEV-SNP's hardened design still leaks through deterministic ciphertext, and "AEPIC Leak" (USENIX 2022) demonstrated an architectural (not merely microarchitectural) leak of uninitialized data. Meanwhile the frontier expanded to accelerators and real-time systems with "StrongBox: A GPU TEE on Arm Endpoints" (CCS 2022) and "RT-TEE" (S&P 2022), signaling that TEEs are now expected to cover GPUs and safety-critical cyber-physical workloads, not just CPU enclaves.
